author: @DESIREDP0V
content:
Spoilers: 








I love the creativity ITS ABSOLUTELY BAFFLING, someone that doesn't normally look into link click intros as I do will not get this but I'd suggest you watch all of it before reading this. 

This whole intro is *NOT* centered around Cheng Xiaoshi but rather it's actually around Lu Guang, it's in his perspective! If you watch the last episode of season two, you understand. Lu Guang wants to save Cheng Xiaoshi by diving back in time to the very beginning!! What do we see in this song? We see the whole song being reversed, seeing Cheng Xiaoshi ascend from the water and Lu Guang starting over again. Then the moment they touch hands, the beat drops, and everything unfolds all over again and this time Lu Guang isn't in the last half of the intro because, Cheng Xiaoshi is the one going through all the hell over and over. Then as  he crashes into the water we see beautiful colors everywhere surrounding him, well those colors represent *blood* and he continues sinking resembling his inevitable end. This shows us that, Lu Guang, no matter how many times he goes back to the very beginning it'll all be the same, he CAN'T change Cheng Xiaoshi's fate.. no matter how many times he goes back to the beginning it all results to the same fate as Cheng Xiaoshi falls through all the chaos meeting his inevitable end.. 1:04

author: @mr.peterpenguinp.2449
content:
Great video, but I disagree with what he said at 6:39. Link Click is more than just entertainment. It reminds you to love and appreciate your family, since you never know when you will lose them. In every single episode/arc, they portray different feelings of love between family (Arc 1 - Emma and her parents, Arc 2 - childhood best friends/lovers, Arc 3 - teammates, crush, mother, etc, Arc 4. missing child and his parents, etc). 

Link Click, as a Chinese anime, has a mostly Chinese audience. So you might need to speak/understand Chinese accurately in order to properly realize just how accurately they portrayed the dialogue and interactions between the characters. The producers put HUGE amount of details in the dialogue. For example in JUST the first episode, you might notice that:
1. Emma’s “country” parents talk to her in an accent while she replied in Mandarin. 
2. Her parents call her “bao bei” (baby/precious) on the phone even though she’s a grown adult (in a really close family, Chinese parents will still call you that even when you’re out of college, I would know :)
3. When Cheng Xiaoshi picks up the phone as Emma, he accidentally calls Emma’s mom “aiyi” or auntie at first because in Chinese culture you call older women your mother’s age aiyi/auntie, even if you don’t know them
4. Emma’s parents calling her late at night to complain that she’s not eating good food is loving and extremely nostalgic. You might’ve heard the stereotype that Asian parents show their love through food, but it’s actually pretty accurate (seeing Emma’s parents give her homemade egg rolls was so heartwarming T-T)
5. At the end of the call, Emma and her parents both say “bye-bye.” Bye bye is not the formal way to say bye in Chinese (which is zai jian) or goodnight (wan an). It’s usually only said to people very close to you, like good friends and family.

And again, just the first episode teaches you a lot about family. Emma’s working away from her parents at her job in a big city, which a lot of Chinese children in the country/rural areas do (as their parents usually aren’t very highly educated, you can kinda stereotypically tell from the accent). She’s often so busy that she doesn’t even have time to have a heartfelt conversation with her parents or even a good dinner. Later after the company went down and her entire career was shattered, she remembered she still had her parents and rushed to meet them. Even if everything in love is going downhill, your mom and dad will still be there to love you and take care of you. 
However in the end, we know what happens. 

Link Click shows how you have to value your family right now, because we don’t know when we might lose them. It convinced me not to work out or study harder, but to take a break from work and school to call my parents for the first time in weeks, to tell my mom and dad how much I love them.

author: @annalisehua
content:
I feel like one of the reasons Link Click isn't that well known or talked about in the west, is as always with stuff from China, their intended, target audience.

Link Click is targeted towards Mainland Chinese millennials and gen Z. This is clear on it's own from the first episode— this is the kind of stuff teens in mainland China in university fears, new workers face, missing home, the vast difference from where they grew up to the city they now live in, caused by the rapidly developing country. This all hits much harder for Chinese teens than any westerners.

And the second, there's the earthquake. 12th May. Any Chinese person would stop and realized the weight of that day. 2008, 12th May. The day where an actual earthquake took place in Mainland China and killed over thousands, destroyed hundreds upon thousands of homes. This hits much, much harder for them, for the people who watched this tragedy happen, who had relatives in the area and with how tight-knit Chinese families are this has a much, much bigger impact than you could've imagined. Everything that sets up to it too. The clouds, the accents of the people, the environment and struggles the people Cheng Xiaoshi had to live through, so many of them are so realistic to them, to us.
Third, all of these stories, are based of real life, actual events in mainland China.
These things have happened. These side stories are real. Someone really lost their son, people actually died in the earthquake on 12th of May 2008. There used to be someone, maybe not named Emma, but have been through the exact same shit. And this hits so much goddamn harder.

Thennnn there's the cultural and language barrier.
China has it's one set of humour, online words and memes that a lot of westerners aren't aware of due to, well, lack of information or misinformation. And honestly it's a hazzle to translate. Then there's the issue of translators. I have... Yet to see a piece of Chinese media translated correctly as in, in a way where there will be no confusion and the original meaning will be preserved without making it awkward or sacrificing it's original humour. There IS a way to do it. But it takes a LOT of time. And honestly? China has a big enough market for companies to earn a shit ton of money, they can care less about what shitty translations westerners get, it's not like they'll appreciate their work, right?
At least, this seems to be the stance they take, judging from their actions.

People have had years to understand and get to know Japanese culture. They understand the humour in animes and the general lives of the Japanese, at least enough to sympathise, to understand slice of life animes from Japan and think they can resonate, they can feel sympathy. China... Doesn't have that. People don't understand the details of Chinese culture, they don't know how the Chinese millennials grew up like the back of their hand, they don't remember specific dates that scarred the entire country. They don't know our legends. People know what Kitsunes are, but do they know who 'zhinu' is? Our culture has been closed off from the world due to misinformation, hate and racism for so long. And this all contributed to our media, now finally gaining some attention, not getting the recognition internationally they deserve.
I hope this sheds light on the entire situation for Donghua. It's a shame that people dismisses these beautiful works of art just like this... Thanks for reading my rant!
Sincerely, someone stuck between two cultures.

author: @HerMan-Winged
content:
In the world of Ling Cage, each faction can be interpreted as representing a different philosophical approach to human survival:
- The Lighthouse faction represents political realism and survival pragmatism.
It has the largest population, so in order to keep society functioning under extreme scarcity, it develops a harsh but sustainable system. The result is a deeply stratified hierarchy where inequality becomes institutionalized. Cruelty is not portrayed as moral, but as a consequence of prioritizing collective survival efficiency.
- Dragonbone Village represents rationalism and long-term civilizational thinking.
With only a few hundred people, this faction is willing to sacrifice a minority — even themselves — for the continuation of humanity as a species. Bai Yuekui embodies this ideology most strongly: survival of future generations justifies the suffering of the present generation. In many ways, this reflects a traditional Confucian-style collectivist mindset often associated with Chinese historical thinking: enduring sacrifice across generations for a greater future.
- Mark represents pure human emotion and moral idealism across all factions.
The narrative clearly frames him as the morally “correct” side — the emotional core and political righteousness of the story. However, what makes the series interesting is that it invites a deeper question:
    If Mark were truly placed in charge of either the Lighthouse or Dragonbone Village, could humanity actually survive?
    Perhaps the Lighthouse, under a more equal and compassionate distribution system, would collapse from starvation even faster.
    Perhaps Dragonbone Village, without the willingness to sacrifice individuals and endure immense hardship, would never complete the extremely long-term plan required to eradicate the Mana ecosystem.
What makes Ling Cage compelling is that it does not simply present a battle between “good” and “evil.” Instead, it explores the tension between realism, rationalism, and humanity itself — forcing the audience to confront whether moral purity alone is enough to ensure the survival of civilization.
